common_name: Dea Hens and Chicks (Jade-Green to Pink Historic Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; strong light is needed to bring out the pink and burgundy flush.

directions: 'Dea' is a long-established European hens and chicks selection that forms unusually large, tightly packed rosettes of broad, fleshy leaves shifting from jade green to rosy pink or burgundy depending on season and light. Full sun and lean, mineral soil bring out the strongest pink coloring, while shade or overly rich ground keeps the rosettes mostly green. Like other sempervivums it spreads readily by stolon-borne offsets, forming a dense ground-covering mat over time, and each individual rosette is monocarpic, flowering once on a short pink spike before dying back. Sharp drainage matters more than winter cold for keeping this cold-hardy alpine succulent healthy through wet seasons.

common_name: Bunny Girl Hens and Chicks (Velvety Gray-Green to Rose-Purple Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; the fine white hairs coating the leaves show up best in bright light.

directions: Grown by specialty nurseries such as Little Prince of Oregon, 'Bunny Girl' forms small, tight rosettes of plump leaves densely covered in fine white hairs, giving the whole plant a soft, velvety texture that shifts from gray-green to rose-purple as the seasons change. The pubescence, unusual among hardy sempervivums, gives it a slightly fuzzy, almost animal-fur appearance that inspired the cultivar name. It offsets freely on short stolons to form a tidy mat well suited to troughs and crevice plantings, and like other houseleeks each rosette is monocarpic, dying after it sends up a single summer flower stalk. Plant in extremely well-drained, gritty soil in full sun, since excess winter moisture is a far greater threat than cold.

common_name: Mona Lisa Hens and Chicks (Light Green Flushing Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; cooler temperatures in late winter and early spring intensify the red flush.

directions: 'Mona Lisa' forms tight, symmetrical rosettes of light green leaves that flush a bright, glowing red in late winter and early spring before settling back toward green as temperatures warm, a seasonal color shift that makes it a favorite for trough and rock garden displays. It stays compact and offsets readily from short stolons, filling in bare crevices and building a dense colony over a few seasons. As with all hardy houseleeks, individual rosettes are monocarpic, sending up a single flowering stalk before dying, but the surrounding chicks continue the display uninterrupted. Grow in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun, where sharp drainage protects against winter rot far more than cold protects against frost damage.

common_name: El Toro Hens and Chicks (Large Rose-Purple-Tipped Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; larger rosette size benefits from slightly more spacing than typical hens and chicks.

directions: An older, historic garden selection still grown by specialty nurseries, 'El Toro' produces unusually large rosettes of pointed green leaves tipped in rose-purple, standing out among many finer-textured houseleek cultivars for its bold scale. It holds its size and color best in full sun and lean, mineral soil, becoming looser and greener in shade or overly fertile ground. Offsets form readily around the mother rosette on short stolons, gradually building a substantial clump, though each flowering rosette dies after blooming in the classic monocarpic pattern of the genus. Sharp drainage is essential through winter, since standing moisture is a far greater threat to this cold-hardy alpine succulent than freezing temperatures.

common_name: Red Lion Hens and Chicks (Belgian Glossy Red Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, which keeps the glossy red coloring saturated through the growing season.

directions: This Belgian-bred cultivar forms low, wide rosettes of glossy, rich red leaves with green tips that hold their vivid color across the growing season better than many red-toned houseleeks, which often fade or bronze in heat. It multiplies vigorously from stolon-borne offsets each spring, quickly forming a dense, colorful mat suited to rock gardens, troughs, and green roofs. Grow in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun; like other sempervivums, individual rosettes flower once and die, but new chicks continuously replace them.

common_name: Green Wheel Hens and Chicks (Symmetrical Apple-Green Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; this compact selection stays neat with minimal grooming.

directions: RHS-listed 'Green Wheel' forms small, remarkably symmetrical rosettes of bright apple-green leaves arranged in an even, wheel-like pattern that gives the cultivar its name. It stays compact and neat with age rather than sprawling, and sends out offsets on notably long, hot-pink stolons that make the propagating chicks almost as ornamental as the parent rosette. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, where its clean green color and tidy habit make it a reliable edging plant for troughs and rock gardens. As with all hardy houseleeks, each individual rosette blooms once on a summer flower stalk and then dies, leaving the spreading offsets to carry on.

common_name: Corsair Hens and Chicks (Grey-Green to Claret-Red Ciliate Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; summer heat deepens the claret-red coloring.

directions: Documented in the Alpine Garden Society's cultivar encyclopedia, 'Corsair' bears grey-green rosettes of pointed, densely ciliate (fine-haired) leaves that deepen to a rich claret red as summer heat builds, then relax back toward grey-green in cooler weather. The fringe of fine hairs along each leaf margin gives the rosette a slightly textured, frosted edge distinct from smooth-leaved cultivars. It offsets readily to form a spreading mat and, like other sempervivums, each rosette is monocarpic, flowering once before dying while surrounding chicks continue the colony. Plant in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun for the best color contrast between seasons.

common_name: Emerald Giant Hens and Chicks (Large Emerald-Green Purple-Tipped Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into rich, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this selection grows notably larger when given richer soil than most houseleeks tolerate.

directions: True to its name, 'Emerald Giant' produces unusually large rosettes for a hardy sempervivum, holding a bright emerald-green base color with purple-tinged leaf tips that intensify to magenta under cold winter conditions. Unlike most houseleeks, which stay smallest and most colorful in lean, poor soil, this cultivar reaches its largest size when grown in richer ground, though it still requires sharp drainage to avoid rot. It offsets steadily to form a substantial clump, and each individual rosette follows the typical monocarpic sempervivum cycle, flowering once and dying while offsets carry the planting forward. Full sun brings out the strongest color contrast between the green rosette and its purple-flushed tips.

common_name: Pacific Rim Hens and Chicks (Frosted Mint-Green to Plum-Purple Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets into lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; bright light deepens the plum-purple tones.

directions: Part of a Pacific Northwest breeding line, 'Pacific Rim' forms medium rosettes of thick, light green leaves tipped in crimson and dusted with fine silvery hairs, giving a soft, frosted look that shifts toward plum-purple under strong sun. It stays green-blue and calmer in cooler, lower-light conditions, making its coloring a useful indicator of how much sun a planting is receiving. It offsets freely to build a tidy clump or spreading mat, and like other hardy houseleeks each rosette blooms once on a summer flower stalk before dying, with the surrounding chicks continuing the display. Grow in lean, extremely well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest color development.

common_name: Party Platter Aeonium (Flat Bright-Green Saucer-Rosette Hybrid)

planting.note: Root offsets or basal cuttings in fast-draining succulent mix after callusing; grow in full sun to light afternoon shade for the flattest, most saucer-like rosette form.

directions: A hybrid of Aeonium arboreum and one of the flat-rosetted dinner-plate aeoniums, 'Party Platter' forms a wide, shiny, bright green disc of overlapping, mosaic-like leaves that hugs low to the ground much like the classic dinner-plate types but grows more easily and vigorously than those species. The short stem stays largely hidden beneath the spreading rosette, with basal offsets forming around its edge for propagation. Because it rarely flowers in cultivation, cuttings and offsets are the main way to propagate it true to form. Grow in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates, watering during the cool-season active growth period and letting the mix dry out in summer dormancy.

common_name: Shozoden Gasteria (Petite Green-and-Yellow Variegated Clumping Succulent)

planting.note: Pot offsets in gritty, well-drained succulent mix and grow in bright indirect light or dappled shade; protect from frost and from direct midday sun, both of which stress this small variegated cultivar.

directions: Of likely G. gracilis or G. minima parentage, 'Shozoden' is a nursery-selected variegated Gasteria with small, fleshy, tongue-shaped leaves striped and speckled in green and yellow, staying notably more compact than most species in the genus. It clumps densely and quickly from basal offsets, making it well suited to shallow dish gardens and small pots on a shaded windowsill. Reddish-pink, green-mouthed flowers appear on a slender stalk from winter into spring. Give it bright, indirect light rather than direct sun, which scorches the thin variegated leaves, and water only when the gritty mix has dried out completely, since like other Gasteria it is highly susceptible to rot in constantly damp soil.

common_name: White Sprite Cotyledon (Grey-Green Finger-Leaf Succulent with Magenta Tips)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in fast-draining, mineral-heavy succulent mix after callusing; grow in full sun for the strongest magenta leaf-tip color.

directions: 'White Sprite' is an upright-growing Cotyledon cultivar bearing long, slender, finger-like leaves in soft grey-green that flush magenta at the tips when grown in bright, direct sun, an effect that fades to plain grey-green in shadier spots. Its narrow leaf form and branching habit give it a more slender, architectural silhouette than the broader-leaved pig's ear selections common in cultivation. Pendant, bell-shaped orange-red flowers appear on upright stalks in fall, adding late-season color when many succulents have finished blooming. Grow in gritty, mineral-rich, fast-draining soil in full sun and water only once the mix has dried completely, propagating easily from stem cuttings allowed to callus before rooting.
